parole.significato: A plant of the obsolete genus Azalea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Azalea, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos, “dry”), because it grows in dry soil; from ἄζω (ázō, “to dry up”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-.

parole.significato: Any of several passerine birds in the genus Batis, related to wattle-eyes.
parole.testo: From translingual Batis, the genus in question, itself likely from Ancient Greek βατίς (batís).

parole.significato: Any fish in the family Batrachoididae, the toadfishes.
parole.testo: From translingual Batrachoididae, from Ancient Greek βάτραχος (bátrakhos, “frog”).

parole.significato: Any fungus of the genus Botrytis, especially Botrytis cinerea which is responsible for the formation of noble rot on gr…
parole.testo: From translingual Botrytis. Blend of Ancient Greek βότρυς (bótrus) + -itis, from Ancient Greek βότρυς (bótrus, “(bunch of) grapes”) + -itis (“disease”) (from New Latin -itis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”)).

parole.significato: Any plant of the division Bryophyta, defined sensu lato to comprise the mosses, liverworts and hornworts and correspond…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Bryophyta, from Ancient Greek βρύον (brúon, “moss”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant”) ( + -phyte).

parole.significato: Any leaf beetle of the family Chrysomelidae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Chrysomelidae, from the type genus of Chrysomela, from the root word of Ancient Greek χρῡσόμηλον (khrūsómēlon).

parole.significato: Related to cnidarians or their stinging cells.
parole.testo: From translingual Cnidaria, from Ancient Greek κνίδη (knídē, “nettle”).

parole.significato: A capsule, in certain cnidarians, containing a barbed, string-like tube that transfers a paralyzing sting.
parole.testo: From translingual Cnidaria, from Ancient Greek κνίδη (knídē, “nettle”) + -cyte (“cell type”).

parole.significato: Any of the fungi of the genus Cordyceps, a genus of endoparasitoid sac fungi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Cordyceps, from Ancient Greek κορδῡ́λη (kordū́lē, “club”) + -ceps (“headed”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Crataegus, the hawthorns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Crataegus, from Ancient Greek κράταιγος (krátaigos, “Crataegus heldreichii”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Crinum of perennial plants with large showy flowers on leafless stems, which develop from bulbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Crinum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κρῐ́νον (krĭ́non, “lily”).

parole.significato: Any one of least 50 species of shrub in the genus Daphne of the family Thymelaeaceae, some of which are grown as orname…
parole.testo: From translingual Daphne, from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē, “laurel”).

parole.significato: A medium agile dinosaur, of the genus Deinonychus, of the Cretaceous period, characterized by having a large, curved cl…
parole.testo: From translingual Deinonychus (1969), from Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “fearful, terrible”) (see dinosaur) + ὄνυξ (ónux, “nail, claw, talon”).

parole.significato: A cultivated plant, belonging to the genus Delphinium, with tall blue-colored spikes containing flowers; a larkspur.
parole.testo: From the genus name (translingual Delphinium), from Ancient Greek δελφῐ́νῐον (delphĭ́nĭon, “larkspur”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Demodex of mites.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Demodex, from Ancient Greek δημός (dēmós, “fat”, noun) + δήξ (dḗx, “worm in wood”).

parole.significato: Any brown alga of the genus Dictyota.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dictyota, from Ancient Greek δικτυωτός (diktuōtós, “netted; latticed”).

parole.significato: Venus flytrap
parole.testo: From translingual Dionaea, from Ancient Greek Διωναία (Diōnaía), a name of Aphrodite.

parole.significato: Any longhorn beetle of the genus Dorcadion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dorcadion, itself from Ancient Greek δορκάδιον (dorkádion), a diminutive form of Ancient Greek δορκᾰ́ς (dorkắs, “roe, gazelle, antelope”).

parole.significato: Possessing a palatal structure akin to the emu and the other (now extinct) species of the genus Dromaius.
parole.testo: Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley: binomial translingual Dromæus (“Dromaius”) (from Ancient Greek δρομαῖος (dromaîos, “swift-running”)) + Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”) + English -ous, adjectival suffix

parole.significato: A stem plant that completes its entire life cycle submerged, or with only its flowers above the waterline.
parole.testo: From translingual Elodea, from Ancient Greek ἑλώδης (helṓdēs, “marshy”), from ἕλος (hélos, “marsh”)

parole.significato: Any of a genus Encrinus of fossil encrinoidea from the Mesozoic rocks.
parole.testo: From translingual Encrinus, from Ancient Greek ἐν- (en-, “in”) + κρίνον (krínon, “lily”).

parole.significato: Any of several protists, of the genus Euglena, that contain chloroplasts and a single flagellum.
parole.testo: From translingual Euglena, from Ancient Greek εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + γλήνη (glḗnē, “eye”).

parole.significato: Any mammal in the order Artiodactyla, including camels, pigs and ruminants such as deer, cattle, goats, sheep and antel…
parole.testo: From even-toed (as a translation of the taxonomic name, translingual Artiodactyla, from Ancient Greek ἄρτιος (ártios, “even in number”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “toe”)) + ungulate.

parole.significato: Any of various orchids with helmet-shaped flowers, of genera Coryanthes, Corybas, Cranichis, Nematoceras, and Pterostyl…
parole.testo: Calque of translingual Corybas, though an incorrect calque, as the taxonomic name is from Ancient Greek Κορῠ́βᾱς (Korŭ́bās), not κόρῠς (kórŭs, “helmet”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus †Hypsilophodon of small ornithopod herbivorous dinosaurs.
parole.testo: From the genus name translingual Hypsilophodont. By surface analysis, hypsi- + loph- + -odont, from Ancient Greek ὑψίλοφος (hupsílophos).

parole.significato: Any fishlike marine reptiles of the extinct order †Ichthyosauria of the early Triassic to the late Cretaceous period, t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Ichthyosaurus, equivalent to Ancient Greek ἰχθύς (ikhthús, “fish”) + Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).

parole.significato: A member of the genus Ixodes of ticks.
parole.testo: Back-formation from translingual Ixodes, from Ancient Greek ἰξώδης (ixṓdēs).

parole.significato: Any bacterium of the genus Leptospira.
parole.testo: From translingual Leptospira, from Ancient Greek λεπτός (leptós, “thin”) + σπεῖρα (speîra, “coil”).

parole.significato: Any butterfly of the genus Lycaena.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from translingual Lycaena, from Ancient Greek λῠ́καινᾰ f (lŭ́kaină, “she-wolf”).

parole.significato: A club moss of the genus Lycopodium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Lycopodium, from Ancient Greek λύκος (lúkos, “wolf”) + πούς (poús, “foot”), equivalent to lyco- + -podium.

parole.significato: Any plant bug in the family Lygaeidae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Lygaeidae, from the type genus, translingual Lygaeus, borrowed from Ancient Greek λῡγαῖος (lūgaîos, “dark, gloomy”).

parole.significato: Any of the spiny-tailed lizards of the genus Uromastyx.
parole.testo: From translingual Mastigurus (“genus Uromastyx”), from Ancient Greek μάστιξ (mástix, “a scourge, a whip”) + οὐρά (ourá, “a tail”). Compare Uromastyx. By surface analysis, mastigo- + -ure (“tail”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Morpho of large tropical American butterflies.
parole.testo: From the genus name, translingual Morpho, from Ancient Greek μορφώ (morphṓ, “the Shapely One”) (a name of Aphrodite).

parole.significato: Any of the small deep-sea fish of the large family Myctophidae, known for their conspicuous use of bioluminescence.
parole.testo: From translingual Myctophidae, from Ancient Greek μυκτήρ (muktḗr, “nose”) + ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”).

parole.significato: A worm of the large phylum Nematoda, such as a roundworm or threadworm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Nematoda, from Ancient Greek νηματώδης (nēmatṓdēs, “fibrous, in filaments”), from νῆμα (nêma, “thread, yarn”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs, “-like”).

parole.significato: Any of various ground-nesting halictid bees of the genus Nomia, native to Asia, many species of which have opalescent b…
parole.testo: From translingual Nomia, from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture, meadow - their typical habitat”) + -ia.

parole.significato: The takahe, Porphyrio mantelli, a flightless rail native to New Zealand.
parole.testo: From translingual Notornis (“a genus name”), from Ancient Greek νότος (nótos, “south”) + ὄρνις (órnis, “bird”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Ochna of evergreen trees, shrubs and shrublets.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Ochna, from Ancient Greek ὄχνη (ókhnē, “pear tree”).

parole.significato: Any mammal in the order Perissodactyla, including horses and other equids, rhinoceroses, and tapirs.
parole.testo: From odd-toed (as a translation of the taxonomic name, translingual Perissodactyla, from Ancient Greek περισσός (perissós, “odd in number”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “toe”)) + ungulate.

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Onosma, of the family Boraginaceae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Onosma, from Ancient Greek ὄνοσμᾰ (ónosmă).

parole.significato: Any orchid of the genus Ophrys, often vernacularly called bee orchids.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Ophrys, from Ancient Greek ὀφρῡ́ς (ophrū́s, “eyebrow”); further from Proto-Hellenic *opʰrū́s and Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰrúHs. Doublet of bree and brow.

parole.significato: A platypus (genus Ornithorhynchus).
parole.testo: From translingual Ornithorhynchus (genus name), from Ancient Greek ὄρνῑς (órnīs, “bird”)) + Ancient Greek ῥύγχος (rhúnkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: Any leguminous plant of the genus Oxylobium, also commonly called shaggy peas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Oxylobium, from translingual oxy- (“sharp”, Ancient Greek ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s)) + Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós, “lobe”) + translingual -ium, literally “sharp-lober”.

parole.significato: Synonym of locoweed.
parole.testo: From translingual Oxytropis, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, pointy”) + τρόπις (trópis, “keel”).

parole.significato: Any of various flowering plants of the genus Pelargonium, similar to (and often confused with) true geraniums, but less…
parole.testo: From translingual Pelargonium, from Ancient Greek πελαργός (pelargós, “stork”).

parole.significato: Any of several Australian dasyurid marsupials, of the genus Phascogale, the males of which die shortly after mating.
parole.testo: From genus name, translingual Phascogale (from Ancient Greek φάσκωλος (pháskōlos, “pouch, wallet”) + γαλέη (galéē, “weasel”)), classified 1824 by Dutch zoologist Coenraad Jacob Temminck.

parole.significato: An insect, Daktulosphaira vitifoliae of the family Phylloxeridae (not the genus Phylloxera), that is very destructive t…
parole.testo: From the original, superseded genus name translingual Phylloxera, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”) + ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

parole.significato: Any of many parasitic pseudofungi, of the genus Phytophthora, that cause brown rot in plants.
parole.testo: From the translingual Phytophthora (genus name), from Ancient Greek φῡτόν (phūtón, “plant”) + φθορᾱ́ (phthorā́, “destruction, ruin”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Polemonium of gamopetalous perennial herbs.
parole.testo: From the genus name translingual Polemonium, from Ancient Greek πολεμώνιον (polemṓnion), from Πολέμων (Polémōn) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war”) + -ων (-ōn, possessive name suffix).

parole.significato: Any of many plants, of the family Polygonaceae, embracing a large number of species, including bistort, knotweed, smart…
parole.testo: From translingual Polygonum, from Ancient Greek πολύγονον (polúgonon, “knotweed”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γόνυ (gónu, “knee”), so called in allusion to the numerous joints, or neuter of πολύγονος (polúgonos, “prolific”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γόνος (gónos, “offspring”). If the former of

parole.significato: Any snail in the family Polygyridae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Polygyridae, itself from the type genus Polygyra + -idae (taxonomic familial suffix). Further from translingual poly- (“multiple, many”, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús)) + Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “ring, circle”).

parole.significato: Any vine of species Epipremnum aureum, widely cultivated as a houseplant, once classified in the genus Pothos.
parole.testo: From translingual Pothos, the genus name. The similarity to Ancient Greek Πόθος (Póthos), the name of one of Aphrodite's erotes who was said to carry a vine (from πόθος (póthos, “yearning, desire”)) is noted; however, other references give the origin as Sinhalese පෝටා වැල් (pōṭā wæl).

parole.significato: Any of the eukaryotic, usually unicellular organisms—including protozoans, slime molds and some algae—historically grou…
parole.testo: From translingual Protista, from Ancient Greek πρώτιστος (prṓtistos).

parole.significato: Any of the host-specific plant-feeding insects of the family Psyllidae, which feed on plant juices.
parole.testo: From translingual Psyllidae, from Ancient Greek ψύλλα (psúlla).

parole.significato: A parasitic flatworm which needs two hosts to complete its life cycle. The immature form infests freshwater snails and…
parole.testo: From translingual Schistosoma, from Ancient Greek σχιστός (skhistós, “cleaved, divided”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to the genus Spalacolestes
parole.testo: From translingual Spalacolestes + -ine, from Ancient Greek σπᾰ́λᾰξ (spắlăx, “Spalax microphthalmus”) + λῃστής (lēistḗs, “pirate”).

parole.significato: Any of various widely distributed mosses, of genus Sphagnum, which slowly decompose to form peat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Sphagnum, which is from Ancient Greek σφάγνος (sphágnos).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to wasps formerly classified in the superfamily Sphecoidea (corresponding to all wasps in Apoidea), no…
parole.testo: From translingual Sphecidae (“taxonomic family of wasps”), from Ancient Greek σφήξ (sphḗx, “wasp”).

parole.significato: Any of the sand wasps of Sphex and allied genera.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Sphex, from the Ancient Greek σφήξ (sphḗx, “wasp”), plural σφῆκες (sphêkes). The plural spheges is likely a borrowing from Latin Sphēgēs.

parole.significato: Any conch of the genus Strombus. Most subspecies are known as forms of fighting conchs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Strombus, from Ancient Greek στρόμβος (strómbos, “shell, conch, snail”).

parole.significato: A nematode worm of the family Strongylidae, often parasitic in the gastrointestinal tract of mammals, especially horses
parole.testo: From a translingual taxonomic name derived from the generic name Strongylus, from Ancient Greek στρογγύλος (strongúlos, “round”). Doublet of Estrangelo.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Stylosanthes of flowering plants.
parole.testo: From translingual Stylosanthes, from Ancient Greek στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”) + Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the class Synapsida of animals which have an opening low in the skull roof behind each eye, leaving a bon…
parole.testo: From translingual Synapsida, from syn- + Ancient Greek ἁψίς (hapsís, “arch”).

parole.significato: One of numerous calcareous processes which extend between, and unite, the adjacent septa of certain corals.
parole.testo: From translingual from Ancient Greek συνάπτειν (sunáptein) + -i- + Latin -cula

parole.significato: Any myrtaceous plant of the genus Syzygium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Syzygium, from Ancient Greek συζύγιος (suzúgios, “jointed, connected”).

parole.significato: Any of many extinct primitive amphibians (labyrinthodonts) of the order Temnospondyli, from the Carboniferous, Permian…
parole.testo: From translingual Temnospondyli, from Ancient Greek τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”) + σπόνδυλος (spóndulos), Ionic/Attic form of σφόνδυλος (sphóndulos, “vertebra”).

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of small freshwater fish of the South American family Characidae and West African family Alesti…
parole.testo: From translingual Tetragonopterus, an obsolete genus that included these fish, ultimately from Ancient Greek τετράγωνος (tetrágōnos, “square, quadrilateral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing, fin”).

parole.significato: A carnivorous marsupial (†Thylacinus cynocephalus) which was native to Tasmania, now extinct.
parole.testo: From translingual Thylacinus; from Ancient Greek θύλακος (thúlakos, “pouch, sack”) + Latin -inus (-ine).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Tolype of moths of the Americas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Tolype, from Ancient Greek τολῠ́πη (tolŭ́pē).

parole.significato: Any skipper butterfly of the subfamily Trapezitinae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Trapezitinae. By surface analysis, translingual Trapezites + -ine. Further from Ancient Greek τρᾰπεζῑ́της (trăpezī́tēs, “banker”), τρᾰ́πεζᾰ (trắpeză, “table”), from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥-ped-ih₂- (“tripodal”), comprised of *tri- (“tri-, three”) and *pṓds (“foot”), thems

parole.significato: a parasitic flatworm of the class Trematoda
parole.testo: From translingual Trematoda, from Ancient Greek τρημᾰτώδης (trēmătṓdēs, “having a vent to the intestinal canal”), from τρῆμᾰ (trêmă, “perforation, aperture”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs, “full of, -like”). See also -ode.

parole.significato: Common name of the extinct genus Triceratops; herbivorous ceratopsids from the late Cretaceous.
parole.testo: From translingual Triceratops, from Ancient Greek τρεῖς (treîs, “three”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “face”).

parole.significato: Any of the tropical birds in the genera Xenops, Megaxenops and Microxenops, found in Central and South America.
parole.testo: From translingual Xenops, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Any one of several of South African lizards of the genus Zonurus (now Smaug), common in rocky environments.
parole.testo: From translingual Zonurus, from zon- (“girdle, belt”), from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”) + -urus (“-tailed”), from Ancient Greek οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).
